steps.say: An agent that watches a running kernel, writes its own eBPF controls, and blocks an exploit while the service keeps running.
That is the pitch. The repository holds the bottom of this picture.
steps.caption: Programmable kernel and network (eBPF)

scenes.headline: Shirudo: signed shields for a running kernel
scenes.sub: What a shield is, and how it gets in
scenes.say: I'm Bastion. Shirudo is the path an agent's code has to pass through before it touches a kernel. Let's follow one shield through it.

scenes.title: A shield is a few lines of BPF

steps.say: This one guards Copy Fail, a bug in the kernel's crypto sockets. It sits on a security hook, the one every socket creation passes.
Any crypto socket is refused. The exploit is gone, and so is every honest use of the socket family.
steps.term: LSM hook: where the kernel asks permission

heads: No shield: the exploit reaches the page cache
A detector counts, and refuses nothing
Block AF_ALG: every crypto socket refused
Block splice: only zero-copy sends refused

rows.label: AEAD decrypt with a bad tag
Hash a file by splicing it
Splice page cache, force a failed decrypt

steps.say: Six kinds of traffic. With no shield, the splice into a failing decrypt writes on a page the socket does not own.
The repo's detector only counts. Run it first, and you learn who splices into these sockets before you block anything.
The blunt shield stops the exploit at socket creation, and four honest callers with it.
The precise one waits for the send and refuses only zero-copy splices. The comment says why it can't be narrower: the operation lives in a struct with no type information.

scenes.credit: Isovalent, Cisco and OpenAI introduce Shirudo

steps.say: The operator host holds the only signing key. It compiles the shield into a signed loader, a program that loads the shield from inside the kernel.
The registry just stores bytes. Shirudo does not trust it.
The target holds only the public certificate. Its kernel checks the signature, and a gate refuses every other BPF load, even from root.
A changed byte fails here, before the kernel sees anything.
A file re-signed with someone else's key fails here.
A shield built for a kernel that renamed a field fails here.
And if the TPM refuses the measurement, the load is undone. Every load and unload is on the record.

scenes.label: BPF time the guards add to a fork and exec
scenes.note: The project's own measurement, in a QEMU guest
scenes.say: It is cheap. The project measured three point two microseconds of guard time on a fork and exec, before any shield of your own.
